requirements.lead_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following:
requirements.req_text: Handling a First Aid Emergency. Do the following: (a) Explain the steps necessary to assess and handle a first aid emergency, including a safety evaluation of the scene. (b) Tell how you would obtain emergency medical assistance from your home and from a remote location on a wilderness camping trip. (c) Demonstrate the precautions you must take to reduce the risk of transmitting an infection between you and the victim while administering first aid, including the safe disposal of used first aid supplies. (d) Demonstrate evaluation of and management of a patient's airway and breathing. (e) Demonstrate a thorough examination of an accident victim. (f) Discuss why shock is an emergency. (g) Define the term triage and describe examples of triage situations that you may encounter.

requirements.req_text: Preparing for First Aid Emergencies. (b) Using checklists provided in the First Aid merit badge pamphlet or ones approved by your counselor, do the following: (1) Assemble a personal first-aid kit for hiking and backpacking. Demonstrate the proper use of each item in your first-aid kit to your counselor. (2) With your counselor, inspect a unit, home, vehicle, or camp first-aid kit and discuss your findings.

pamphlet_excerpts: Bites Mosquitoes Chiggers: The bites of mosquitoes, chiggers, and nosee-ums are irritating but not usuallydangerous.
Troublesome Ticks Spiders: More troublesome are ticks, some spiders, and some ants.
Wear Long Pants: To avoid getting bitten by ticks, wear long pants and along-sleeved shirt whenever you are in tickinfested woodlands and fields.
Button Yourcollar Tuck: Button yourcollar and tuck your pant cuffs into yourboots or socks.
step_by_step_procedure: Inspect Yourself Daily: Inspect yourself daily, especially the hairy parts of your body, and immediately remove any ticks you find.
Ticks Bury Their: Ticks bury their heads beneath the skin oftheir victims.
Gloved Hands Grasp: To remove a tick, with gloved hands, grasp it with tweezers close to the skin and gently pulluntil it comes loose.
Don Squeeze Twist: Don’t squeeze, twist, or jerk thetick, as doing so could leave its mouthparts stillburied in the skin.

Anabrasion Wound Occurs: Anabrasion is a wound that occurs as a result of the outer layersof the skin being rubbed or scraped off.
Abrasions Happenwhen Skin: Abrasions may happenwhen the skin is scraped against a hard surface, for example, when a bicyclist falls onto the pavement.
Dirt Gravel Ground: Sometimes dirt and gravel get ground into theabrasion, which increases the likelihood of infection.
step_by_step_procedure: Protect Yourself Cuts: To protect yourself from cuts and scrapes, dress appropriately for the activity, for instance, jeans, boots, gloves, longsleeved shirt.
Few Simple Precautions: A few simple precautions can help you avoid thepain of the treatment and healing process.
Treat Minor Cut: Treat a minor cut or scrape by flushing the area with cleanwater for at least five minutes, or until all foreign matterappears to be washed away.
Remember Protect Yourself: Remember to protect yourself withnonlatex gloves and other precautions as needed, as well asby washing your hands before and after treating.

Victim Care Physician: Get the victim under the care of a physician as soon as possible.
Rewarm Area Onlyif: Rewarm the area onlyif there is no chance of refreezing.
Move Victim Tent: To treat frostnip, move the victim into a tent or building, then warm the injured area.
step_by_step_procedure: Ear Cheek Frozen: If an ear or cheek is frozen, remove a glove and warm the injury with the palm of yourhand.
Slip Frostnipped Hand: Slip a frostnipped hand under your clothing and tuckit beneath an armpit.
Treat Frostnipped Toes: Treat frostnipped toes by putting the victim’s bare feet against the warm skin of your belly.
Human Body Percent: The human body is 70 percent water, which is essential tomaintain our body temperature.

pamphlet_excerpts: Cold- Heat-Related: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Heatstroke Heatstroke, much more serious than heat exhaustion, canlead to death if not treated immediately.
Left Untreated: Left untreated, heatexhaustion can develop into heatstroke.
Heatstroke Body Cooling: In heatstroke, the body’s cooling system begins to fail and the person’s coretemperature rises to life-threatening levels (above 105 degrees).
Type Heatstroke Develops: One type of heatstroke develops in young, healthy people fromdehydration and overexertion in hot weather, especially in highhumidity.
step_by_step_procedure: Sign True Heat: The first sign of true heat stroke is often collapse.
Hot Day Someone: On a hot day, if someone collapses without warning, you mustconsider heatstroke.
Type Heatstroke Happens: The other type of heatstroke usually happens in elderlypeople when the weather is very hot, especially with highhumidity.
Signals Similar: The signals are similar to exercise-related heatstrokeexcept that the skin is hot and dry because there is no sweating.

pamphlet_excerpts: Cold- Heat-Related: Cold- and Heat-Related Conditions and Injuries Heatstroke Heatstroke, much more serious than heat exhaustion, canlead to death if not treated immediately.
Left Untreated: Left untreated, heatexhaustion can develop into heatstroke.
Heatstroke Body Cooling: In heatstroke, the body’s cooling system begins to fail and the person’s coretemperature rises to life-threatening levels (above 105 degrees).
Type Heatstroke Develops: One type of heatstroke develops in young, healthy people fromdehydration and overexertion in hot weather, especially in highhumidity.
step_by_step_procedure: Sign True Heat: The first sign of true heat stroke is often collapse.
Hot Day Someone: On a hot day, if someone collapses without warning, you mustconsider heatstroke.
Type Heatstroke Happens: The other type of heatstroke usually happens in elderlypeople when the weather is very hot, especially with highhumidity.
Signals Similar: The signals are similar to exercise-related heatstrokeexcept that the skin is hot and dry because there is no sweating.

requirements.req_text: Do ONE of the following: (a) Visit an emergency medical station house or training center in person. From the medical first responders that you meet during your visit, learn about how they serve their community and about their careers. Discuss with your counselor what you learned during your tour and interviews. (b) Interview an emergency medical services professional about their work. Learn about how they chose this career and about their duties. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (c) Identify three career opportunities that would use skills and knowledge in emergency medical services. Pick one and research the training, education, certification requirements, experience, and expenses associated with entering the field. Research the prospects for employment, starting salary, advancement opportunities, and career goals associated with this career. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and whether you might be interested in this career. (d) Identify how you might use the skills and knowledge in the field of emergency medical services to pursue a personal hobby and/or healthy lifestyle. Research the additional training required, expenses, and affiliation with organizations that would help you maximize the enjoyment and benefit you might gain from it. Discuss what you learned with your counselor and share what short-term and long-term goals you might have if you pursued this.
